My hon. friend tells us
that he was the heir of obligations and burdens. In spite of these obligations and burdens he went on to claim that he had larger surpluses and had reduced debts more than his predecessors had ever been able to do. Does my hon. friend really deceive himself so much in the case of-I do

not want to use a strong word-self-concentration in which he is bound up? Does he deceive himself to the extent of thinking that he had anything to do with these surpluses? Does he deceive himself to the extent of thinking now that his Government in the first two years they were in office, had anything to do in providing surpluses? Is he quite fair in blaming his predecessors for his obligations and burdens and pluming himself upon the surpluses and reduction of debt? Surely it is a fair argument that for the first two years this Government was in power, if they received the obligations and burdens that their predecessors sent down to them, they received from their predecessors the money with which careful financiers would have tackled those obligations.
My hon. friend when he boasts of those surpluses, reminds me of the younger son of a distinguished family who asked that the portions of goods coming to him might be given to him, and then took himself into a far country. I have no doubt that the associates with whom he foregathered there thought that as long as his money lasted, that that younger son was an admirable financier; hut when he got among the husks no doubt they formed a different opinion of him. There is this to be said of the prodigal, that experience in his case was a wise teacher and sweet were the uses of adversity. But the experience which produced in the prodigal son a salutary attack of penitence has had an effect upon my hon. friend which resulted in a lamentable exhibition of ill-humour and egotism.
With regard to the comparison of the two Governments, there is this to be said about the previous Government-that if they were extravagant they had the money to do it with. That is a statement the accuracy of which I think the hon. gentleman will not deny. Now, I am against extravagance whether in prosperous times or in adverse times. I learned some of my finance from the speeches I used to hear from my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) when he was in Opposition. I found him a good financier; I found in his speeches many words of wisdom, following up lessons in finance which I had learned from the greatest financier^ in the old country. I am against extravagance whether on the part of the Government or on the part of an individual, and whether in adversity or in prosperity. But if I have to choose between a Government spending an income which it has and a Government borrowing to spend, I prefer the former. The difference between 55i
the two is that between a successful man of business and a man who is in the hands of the money-lenders and who borrows to pay interest on previous borrowings. That is what I have to say in regard to my hon. friend's tu quoque argument. There are other points in what he said this afternoon to which I hope to refer before I resume my seat, but I do not propose to be drawn away by, what for want of a better word I may call, his arguments from looking at the present conditions of the country as revealed in the Budget, and the proposals for relieving that condition.
i' submit, Mr. Speaker, that the Budget statement of my hon. friend revealed a lamentable condition of finance in this country. And unfortunately it is true that the lamentable condition of finance revealed by the Budget finds a reflection in the conditions of our people outside of
10	p.m. this Chamber. Deficits and debt in Parliament are accompanied by poor trade and a good deal of destitution and unemployment among the people. The Minister of Finance has attributed, or has been very anxious apparently to attribute, this condition entirely to the war. Well, I like to be candid, I like to be fair; and I am bound to say that in my humble judgment conditions have been aggravated by the war. I do not think it possible to deny that the conditions have been agravated by the war. But there is a possibility for two opinions as to how far the war has operated in this direction. The Minister of Finance talks as if there was no possibility of an argument upon this subject. I should like to point out to hon. gentlemen opposite that a very distinguished member of this House, the hon. member for West Toronto (Sir Edmund Osier) has made a public speech in which he strongly states an opposite opinion. And, after all, we cannot brush to one side an opinion on a financial question uttered by the hon. member for West Toronto. That hon. gentleman was an authority on finance in this country before the Minister of Finance had ceased wearing long clothes. The hon. member for West Toronto made a speech in which he said that conditions had been saved in this country by the war, that orders had come to this country which had put business in motion and which meant $200,000,000 to the common people. In any case, I want to point out this in answer to the argument advanced by the Minister of Finance: to prove his point that the finances of this country have been thrown into disorder almost entirely by. the war, what did he do? He quoted the trade figures of

Australia to prove that in Australia a similar condition of affairs had come about.
He quoted the trade figures of the United States to show that the war had brought about the same condition of affairs there. I understood my hon. friend to state-I should like his attention upon this point and correction if I am/wrong-that in both Australia and the United States the figures of imports were showing an increase before the war. Has it not occurred to my hon. friend that there is a very striking difference on that point between Canada and these other countries? I should have thought that candour and courage in argument would have led my hon. friend at that point to deal with the unanswerable figures given by the hon. junior member for Halifax. The hon. member for Halifax quoted the figures of our import trade from January of last year down to August of last year, when war broke out, and by those figures he showed that contrary to what was the case in Australia and the United States, month by month, through January, February, March, April, May, June, July, there was an average decrease in the imports into Canada of over $10,000,000 a month. Surely those figures needed to be met. What did my hon. friend say with regard to that argument? Not a syllable. He did not controvert them, because they were incontrovertible proof that bad times were severely upon Canada before the war came at all. My hon. friend shakes his head. Was a decline of over $10,000,000 a month in the imports not a sign that bad times were approaching? It is capable of exact proof that after two and a half years of administration by this Government, when nobody was dreaming of war, there was every evidence that Canada was passing into a condition of commercial depression; and that condition has since been aggravated by the war.
I have on the sheet that is now in my hand some headings of columns which I myself took from newspapers in the month of July last. I took them for a specific purpose. I was going to give an address upon the times, and I took these headings as the best rough and ready evidence I could get of what was the condition of Canada at that time. I find amongst them this heading :	" Canadian Pacific railway stock
reaches a new low level." Canadian Pacific railway stock, worth less, I take it, than it had been for 17 years; less, at any rate, than it had been since it reached its maximum during the 15 years when my right hon. friend was at the head of Government. I find another heading:	"A further large

falling off in customs revenue." Another: " Fifty-three per cent decrease in immigration into the country." Remember that these are all from newspapers published previous to last July. I find another heading :	" Proposed deportation of unemployed." I find in the Canadian Courier, an independent journal, of a date preceding the outbreak of hostilities, a statement to the effect that the most serious problem for Canada at the present is the question of the unemployed. These rough and ready pieces of evidence were found by myself in reading the newspapers of Canada before there was any question of war at all. I take it, Sir, that the hon. Minister of Finance cannot in his light and airy way dispose of that question by saying: in my first year I had a surplus ; in my second year I had a surplus, and in my third year I had the war. Before the war came at all two years had sufficed for this Government to get in its work and they would have proceeded from surpluses to deficits and destitution and unemployment if never a shot had been fired on^he battle field.
It is pertinent, however, to ask hon. gentlemen opposite: why should war produce the bad results in Canada which we all deplore? We still have the home market. As a free trader, I think that is a fair question for me to put to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George. Foster.) Hon. gentlemen opposite have deafened me ever since I came to Canada about the splendid chance of prosperity we get by nursing the home market. Well, there are no German ships or guns here; we still have the home market. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce used to dwell upon the glories of interprovincial trade. We still have interprovincial trade; why should we have hard times? The real value of war from the fiscal standpoint is that it reveals protection in operation. Protection is the sworn foe of foreign commerce, and for the purposes of restricting foreign commerce gun-boats are far more effectual than tariffs. You have protection put in operation by gun boats, and the results do not seem to be to the liking of protectionists, because they say: we have hard times, and the war has produced them. But if they believe in protection; if they believe in their made-in-Canada propoganda, in the home market and in interprovincial trade as the real panacea for the fiscal needs of a country; if they believe in these things, war has just produced what protection would have produced if carried out to its

*logical issue. As I say, they do not like the result; it would be wonderful if they did, for the result proclaims m characters un-mistakeable, so plain that he who runs may read, that the National Policy is a palpable failure. It is a palpable failure as a revenue producer, because it is a palpable failure as a trade producer. There is one point that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance appealed to me on in respect of which I agree with him; that his failure of revenue is due to failure of imports. There we are at one, though I cannot congratulate him in being equally at one with every one on the other side of the House.
I noticed that my hon. friend listened with very great interest and attention and with frequent applause to my hon. friend for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) when he spoke the other day. My hon. friend the member for Muskoka gave it as his deliberate opinion that this country would be very much better off if we reduced very largely both our imports and our exports; or rather, he said we should be as well off as we are now. 1 submit to the member for Muskoka that we are just as well off as we are now because we have reduced both our imports and exports.
I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance might use a little of his spare time to teach elementary economics upon his own side of the House. The National Policy has failed as a revenue producer because it has failed as a trade producer. It is now admitted by my hon. friend that our prosperity was due to borrowing. It was due, as I have frequently contended in this House, to the freest of free imports, and was not due to protective tariffs at all. The National Policy 'has not only failed in these respects; it has failed as an industry builder. For, Mr. Speaker, it is well worthy of remark that for forty years under both political parties-I am not here to defend all that has been done under this head by the Liberal party in the past -we have had the doctrine proclaimed that you must build up cities in this country for that home market to which we are now reduced by the conditions of international trade. We have this peculiar *situation to-day, that the farmers of the country, especially the western farmers, who have never had any real benefit from protection, who cannot have any real benefit from protection because they produce more of their products than are used in the country-they are exporters, and the price of their stuff is as a rule settled abroad-the farmers are reasonably prosperous; not, I think, with all due deference to any hon. friend from Assinboia (Mr. Turriff), as prosperous as he would represent; the price of wheat has gone up; the price of pork at the present moment is very poor in western Canada; the price of beef on the foot Is very poor in western Canada; but still the farmers are getting reasonably good prices; and they are getting them, not by the help of protection, but in spite of it. It is in the towns that we have our destitution; these .towns that have been built up by the National Policy, where industries were to exist, where everybody was to he made prosperous, and upon which the farmers were to depend upon for their prosperity. It would seem, then, that the National Policy is breaking down as a builder of industries. How has this condition been met by v,the Government ? I do not think I have exaggerated;
I should be very sorry to. I hope I am a loyal and patriotic Canadian, though I am only an adopted son in Canada. I do not want to say anything which would hurt my adopted country, any more than I want to say anything to hurt the Empire in the struggle in which she is now engaged. I hope I have not exaggerated.
I have tried to depict fairly what is the condition of this country at the present moment and I turn to ask the question, how has the condition been met ? In regard to the way the Government has met the situation let me quote what the Minister of Finance said concerning our special war expenditures:
I have no hesitation in proposing to the House that we shall borrow the whole amount required under this heading.
Now, that is very -specific language. There was a tendency towards the end of the speech to which we have just listened, for my hon. friend the Minister of Finance rather to qualify and depart from the position which he took in the words:
I have no hesitation in proposing to the House that we shall borrow the whole amount required under this heading.
That is, under the heading of special war expenditure. Very well.
I define absolutely the attitude of hon. members on this side of the House. I say, and not only I say, but it is notorious that we all say: we agree. You are borrowing $100,000,000; we agree. But immediately the Minister of Finance makes that statement, he sets out to give us an account of the whole list of new taxation in the country, the whole series of new taxes, and after

he had got through the description of those taxes he went on in his Budget speech as follows: '
These, Mr. Speaker are the proposals of the Government, having as their object the raising of additional revenue rendered necessary by the war and our participation therein as a belligerent.
Now, it seems to me that these two statements are at variance. Even in the brief speech in which he introduced his Budget my hon. friend was not quite consistent in the two statements he made. The fact is that the case for new taxation is not established. And as I understand the difference on this point between the two sides of the House, I should like to state it thus: the Government proposes to borrow the whole money which they are spending on special war expenditure; we agree. The Government need in addition $7,000,000 for interest and the nucleus of a pension fund. The drain upon the'pension fund cannot be great, fortunately, for some little time to come. As f understand the amendment of my right hon. friend, it raises no objection to getting the money for the interest on the pension fund by some method of direct taxation. I so read the amendment of my right hon. friend, because it would be impossible to speak of direct taxes as burdening the people without giving revenue. I take it, then, that this is the position as between the two sides of the House; with the consensus of both sides the money for the carrying on of the war is being borrowed; the interest and the nucleus of a pension fund are being provided by direct taxation, because my hon. friend only needs $7,000,000 for interest, and the minimum sum he expects to get from direct taxation is $8,000,000, although the Toronto Star has calculated it at $14,000,000. Then where is the justification for the increase of the general tariff and for the obstacles against trade. I hold very strongly-and in this I think we are in general agreement on this utter failure in four hours of talk by the Minister of Finance, and in a great many more hours by hon. gentlemen behind him, to give any justification for increasing the customs taxation at this very serious juncture in the country's history.
. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance rather pooh-poohs the idea of our recommending economy, because when an individual gets hard up or is in straitened circumstances he has to economize. I do not know where my hon. friend learned his l Mr. M. Clark. 1
economics. Personally, I think I can quote very high authorities for the position that a nation's economics should be conducted upon the same principle as an individual's economics. John Bright once said:	" I
make no distinction between the morality that ought to guide a man and that which ought to guide a nation." I take it that moral principles are involved in the way that a man or a nation raises money and spends money. I do not agree with my hon. friend that the nation can learn nothing from the individual in this matter. What is a nation? An aggregate of individuals. Does my hon. friend mean to tell me that a departure from sound economic principles which ruins a man can be undertaken .by a nation? I do not agree wit'h-him for one minute. I stand with John Bright in declaring that the same economic principles in the main which guide a man ought to guide a nation. My hon. friend the junior member for Halifax used a notable phrase in regard to this Government's extravagance. He said that they had exalted extravagance to a virtue. We have had hon. gentlemen getting up in this debate and backing up that kind of thing. They say: The Government must go on spending even if they have to borrow. I wonder when we ever should be economical. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance condemns extravagance on the part of his predecessors who had plenty of money to spend, and he justifies extravagance on his own part when his revenues are falling and when he does not have the money to spend.
I stand in this matter with Cobden. So far from exalting extravagance to the height of virtue, Cobden used the epigram that I remember twice being quoted by Mr. Gladstone, " Public economy is public virtue." If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance had not retired from the House I would have strongly commended that short statement to him. It is very brief, and I have no doubt it has been conveyed to him many, many times by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Geo. Foster), who really cannot view the shortcomings of this mere tyro in finance with anything like equanimity.
Mr. Winston Churchill, who is at the head of a great spending department which might be allowed to be extravagant at the present time if ever a department was-Mr. Winston Churchill, in the midst of the war, making a speech in the House of Commons and

talking of the new departures on the part of the British Admiralty, had this to say:
Everything in our power will be done to avoid extravagance. We shall therefore welcome the advice of businessmen where they can help us.
As my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, the Government of Great Britain calls to their assistance the Opposition in the House of Commons and in the House of Lords, and Mr. Winston Churchill also has asked that he should have the advice of any business men who could help him to conduct the great spending department of the Admiralty on economical lines. The Minister of Finance, when he was constructing his Budget, instead of calling to his councils the Opposition, and especially my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, whose long experience in Government would enable him to give much valuable information and advice, appears to have consulted with the Canadian manufacturers.
My hon. friend the junior member for Halifax, in arraigning this Government, was interrupted by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister with a question and the question of my right hon. friend reminded me of a celebrated programme called the Halifax programme. I was surprised at my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, because I remember reading that modern evangel promulgated in the city of Halifax, and I remember many expositions of it by my right hon. friend. I do not apologize for quoting the statement which was made in one of these expositions by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to the effect that an expenditure of a little over $100,000,000 by the late Government was prima facie evidence that the Government was corrupt. When my hon. friend the Finance Minister, or any other hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, turns and asks us where he could begin economizing I think it is a perfectly logical procedure on his part to consult the Prime Minister. He must have had some ideas, if he was sincere, when he promulgated this gospel. I was surprised at his addressing his colleague in the representation of Halifax and putting to him the question as to whether he would consent to begin economizing in the city of Halifax. If he had been as sincere as the early projectors of the original evangel, who began at Jerusalem, Halifax is the very place that he would have begun to put into practice the gospel which he preached previous to 1911.
I appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the best of good humour, because I am perfectly sure that he has had many a serious interview with this Cabinet. I told him when he joined it that he was a. schoolmaster amongst children, that he was the only gentleman who had had any previous Cabinet experience, and the country is paying dearly for the fact, because he has been utterly powerless either by advice or example to restrain those with whom he is associated. My hon. friend in the year 1908, with an expenditure of about $108,000,000 for current and capital account, made a speech in this House in which he said:
The rapid pace that has been set and the recklessness ot the expenditures that have been undertaken have obliterated all the old rules, all the old lines in reference to expenditure.
If that was the case with an expenditure of $108,000,000 a year what are- we to say about the old lines and the old rules when the expenditure for the same object has got up to $160,000,000? Then, plaintively in that address, after making this statement he asks:	Whither are we
rushing? I wonder if he ever addresses that inquiry to his colleagues in the Cabinet. If not I would strongly urge him to do so and especially to try and enforce the inquiry upon the present holder of the portfolio of Finance. The fact of the matter is that the Prime Minister made a fatal error in the original composition of his Cabinet, and I would advise him at once, if he wants to guide this country through to a saner and stronger financial position, to transpose a certain couple of ministers. The Minister of Finance would have made a splendid Minister of Trade and Commerce. Especially would he have excelled in the performance of the duties of the Department of Trade and Commerce which are described as those of the chief commercial traveller of Canada. The Minister of Finance has a smile that my hon. friend without portfolio opposite knows would be valuable in a commercial traveller, but a smile is no good to a watch dog. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has a smile, but he wears it in his heart. My hon. friend, if he had been given the portfolio of Finance and had been entrusted with the proper duties as the watch dog of the treasury, would have kept his smile most effectually when his present neighbour, the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) and others came to him to make the drains for their spending departments which have landed the country in the posi-

tion in which it is in at the present time. But the Government do not see fit to appeal to the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce for lessons in economy. They do not wish to have them put in practice at the present time, and they have decided upon other proposals.
Let me say at once that the proposals of taxation which the Finance Minister has brought down for the approval of this House are absolutely lacking in initiative. I congratulate the Government upon their direct taxation; I congratulate them on embarking on direct taxation at all. The imposition of direct taxes is a very joyful spectacle for one who has been preaching the economic doctrines that I have been preaching in Canada for a number of years past. I have heard many men, since I came to Canada, ask: Where would you get your revenues if you established free trade and do awa"y with tariffs? the people of this country would never stand for direct taxation; you will not have it for generations. Well, Mr. Speaker, war is a fine fiscal schoolmaster, and the war has brought us to a position in which this country has gone in for direct taxation, and I congratulate the Government upon introducing it. But the choice of the Minister of Finance in regard to his direct taxes has, as my right hon. leader has pointed out, not been quite fortunate. . He has passed his direct taxes almost in every case right on to the consumers of the country, and to that extent he has failed to carry out direct taxation as it is carried out in the old country where the greatest burden is borne by the people who are most able to pay the taxes.
I think the Minister of Finance offered to the House, both when he introduced his Budget and again to-day, an extremely weak argument in opposition to an income tax. When he introduced his Budget he said that the income tax in Great Britain was mostly gathered upon huge investments. My recollection is that the minimum income paying tax in England is $1,000 a year, and I do not think the Minister of Finance is correctly informed in making the statement he did. I pointed out a year ago, I think in my Budget remarks, that at that time an income tax had been imposed in the United States, an income tax existed in Germany, that an income tax existed in France, and that surely the statesmanship of Canada was not absolutely so deficient that it could not come near the statesmanship of these various countries. I noticed the other day Russia, one of the Allies, had imposed an

income tax for war purposes, and the minimum income paying the tax is $500 per annum. If our Allies are doing this, I do not see why Canada should not have put on a good fat tax upon large incomes, and I want to say that while such a tax would have this merit that it followed the example of all other civilized countries of the world, it would have had the approbation of the great masses of the people of Canada. It is a fair tax because accordihg to the first principle of taxation we ought to gather our taxes as much as possible in proportion to the ability of the tax-payer to pay. I am perfectly certain that a good fat tax upon big incomes would have been a popular form of taxation, and a better form of taxation than many of the vqxatious stamp duties which the Minister of Finance has lightly borrowed from the United States. Australia is a country to which we may look for comparison, and sometimes for guidance. Australia is well worthy of imitation in a great many ways. I do not think that hon. gentlemen opposite would be inclined to impugn the loyalty of Australia; I am perfectly sure that they, as we, felt a thrill of joy and satisfaction when the Australian battleship "Sydney" captured the German commerce-destroyer "Emden." What has Australia done in this matter of direct taxation? Australia, for the purposes of this war, has raised $5,000,000 by a federal probate duty, in addition to the probate duty already imposed by the various states.
The Minister of Finance, while commending the courage of the hon. member from Saltcoats (Mr. MaeNutt) for mentioning a land tax, brushed aside a tax upon land values as a thing that was almost unworthy of his consideration. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance knows that Australia, for war purposes, is raising $13,500,000 by a land tax, , in addition to the land taxes gathered by the various states of the Commonwealth. I want to put this
to	the	members of	the	Government,as	well	as	to members	on my ownside	of	the	House,	that	the breakdown of protection in the matter of raising revenue will compel the statesmanship of Canada, sooner or later, as it has compelled the statesmanship of Germany, of the United States, of Russia, of England long ago, to seek direct taxes for carrying on the federal government, leaving the trade of the country free to develop the wealth in the country, which can be taxed as it is in England. Then all your taxation would go to the treasury and none of it to pamper and to feed special interests. I
want to point out tliat land-value taxation is attracting increasing attention in Great Britain and in the United States, where the doctrine of taxation of land values was first promulgated. It has been employed in our own provinces in the West with a very great degree of success, and I want to emphasize the fact which my hon. friend from Saltcoats mentioned: that the grain growers of the prairie provinces, as well as the grange of Ontario and the United Farmers of Ontario have through their delegates in every case unanimously carried a resolution in favour of the taxation of land values in preference to raising additional obstacles against the trade of Great Britain at a time when Great Britain is at war.
Meantime, let me say further about this tariff policy of the Government, that it is a policy lacking not only in initiative, but, I think, lacking in common sense. I will tell you why, because I do not want to use strong language without being able to justify it. The National Policy has failed, else why betake ourselves to direct taxation as the Government has done in this case? The National Policy has failed as a revenue producer, and the policy of the Government is lacking in common sense because they propose to help that failure by more National Policy. I do not think that is a rational procedure. If a medicine is killing every patient that gets it, I do not think it is common sense procedure to administer extra doses of that medicine to the next patient who comes along. It is possible at this juncture to look at the history of tariff in this country. Its history has now been prolonged to such an extent that we can trace the trail of the serpent by the slime it leaves. The National Policy was introduced into this country in 1878. Looking at these years, I have always, since coming to this country, allowed it five years to get into operation, and I have compared the trade of Canada in 1883 with the trade of Canada in 1895, these being the last twelve years that the old Conservative Government was
in power.	.
I have again and again pointed out in this House that in 1895, 17 years after the introduction of the National Policy, the foreign commerce of Canada was smaller by $6,000,000 than it was in 1883, twelve years previously. That is a very significant fact. You yourself, Mr. Speaker, sat in this House at that time, and you saw the trade of the country stationary year after year, until in 1895, after seventeen years of the National Policy, it was lower than it was in 1883,
and the condition of the country generally was in keeping with the trade figures.
The other day I came across a quotation from the News-Advertiser of Vancouver, of February 1, 1895, giving an account of a hoard otf works meeting twenty years ago, in which I read:
Mr. H. A. Ball submitted an elaborate scheme of a poor farm in the Bast End Park where the hungry could be fed and work found for them.
That was after seventeen years o'f the National Policy in Vancouver. That was when the political forefathers of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) were running the affairs of the Dominion. I should think he would recognize a likeness between those times and now. The failure was so evident to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce that, financier and statesman as he was, he faced the situation. What did he do? What my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is doing now-administer more National Policy? No, he reduced the tariff of this country very considerably, although the reduction came too late to save his party. His party went out of power in 1896; my right hon. friend came into power; and despite statements which I have never considered very fair on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite that nothing was done to reduce the tariff during the fifteen years that my right hon. friend was in power, in 1897, following the example, as I freely admit, of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, my right hon. friend reduced the tariff very largely. One hundred and fifty articles were put upon the free list and the British preference was introduced. It is no wonder that my right hon. friend says, as he said this afternoon, " Here we draw the line."
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, forsooth, impugned the motives of my right hon friend as if the British preference were a new thing with him. So far as actual legislation is concerned, my right hon. friend is the father of the British preference in this country. The result of his introduction of the British preference was that just as British goods come here, so British immigrants and British capital come here; and the thing that my hon. friends opposite cannot get over at the present -moment is that, for the fifteen years during which my right hon. friend and his colleagues guided the destinies of Canada, Canada was inhabited by a prosperous, wealthy, contented, and happy people. It goes without saying, that with all

due allowance for the war, the National Policy in a much briefer period had brought about in the beginning of last year when there was not any war the very condition of affairs which existed in this country in 1896, when the upholders of the National Policy were sent about their business, because their policy had proved a failure. What is the cure for this depression? Is it to be more National Policy? Is it to be a made-in-Canada campaign?
Hear, hear.
My hon. friend the member for North Ontario says, " hear, hear." I would like him to go down to Toronto or Montreal and explain his made-in-Canada campaign to the thousands of unemployed there.

I would like my hon.
friend to come to Orillia or any of our towns and say that the made-in-Canada campaign is a stupid policy.

I would not do so without explaining the campaign. Of course, my hon. friend does not understand how stupid it is, but I will explain that point to him. I would like my hon. friend to go to his own city, in which he has spoken in favour of this made-in-Canada campaign, and explain how the National Policy is going to cure the problem that you have resulting from the National Policy which you have followed so far. Let my hon. friend say to one of those unemployed men, of whom there are thousands in the cities throughout Canada; You are having too many imports because that is the meaning of the National Policy campaign. If it means anything, it means that imports are a curse. I do not know what my hon. friends think about imports. If the made-in-Canada campaign has any meaning, it means that you are going to exclude imports. Yet my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us that the country is depressed because we do not have imports any longer. Let any hon. gentleman opposite go to one of the unemployed in Toronto and say: We want fewer imports into this country at the present moment, and let him explain the economics of the policy. If the unemployed man were thoughtful he would say: When Laurier was in power, we were importing largely and we were prosperous; I was getting three good square meals a day then, and I have difficulty in getting them now either for myself or for my family. I imagine that my hon. friend opposite who was on this mission would have to tell that poor workman that he was getung too 
many imports at this time; that they were bad for him; that he needed dieting. He is getting the dieting all right. The imports were all right-the imports into the country accompanied by sufficient imports into the stomachs of the workingmen of the country. There must be a reason for that fact.
I wish I had time to tell hon. gentlemen opposite of some experiences that I had the last time I spoke on protection in England. When I was in England in 1906, I took part in the campaign there. The agitation was along exactly the same lines when Mr. Chamberlain was trying to impose protection upon the old country. His party was telling the people of Great Britain that carpenters were unemployed there because Britain	was	importing too many
window-sashes and doors from Canada. They were having a made-in-Canada campaign in Great Britain. It does not look so well when we see it from this side, does it? Protection is supported by the same fallacies everywhere.
Where	was	the	fallacy? Why	didnot the workingmen of Britain listen to the argument as it was put to them over there? Because teachers who knew something of economics immediately came along and said to the workingmen of Britain:	It is	very	true that	we are	importing	large	numbers of	doors	and
window sashes from Canada; but the peculiar thing is this, that statistics prove that carpenters in Britain have least unemployment when we are importing the most doors. and window-sashes from Canada. Does my hon. friend the member for North Ontario (Mr. Sam. Sharpe) begin to see some light upon the made-in-Canada proposal? Why was it that carpenters were busiest in Britain when they were importing the most doors and window-sashes? Simply because they were busiest in the building trade, and the carpenters of Britain were making better money at hanging the doors made in Canada than they could make in making the doors.
Is there any wise economist on the other side who will tell me that the people of Great Britain do not know their business? Will the hon. member for North Ontario undertake to go to Britain and teach this made-in-Canada policy to Mr. Lloyd George, and improve the narrow fiscal understanding of Mr. Asquith and Sir Edward Grey? I think not.
How will the new tariff act? According to the minister who is responsible for it, it will not only raise revenue, but also promote agriculture and industry. Well, I

never heard a prophecy that I think less likely of fulfilment than that one. If it is going to get revenue, how is it going to promote the made-in-Canada campaign? It is difficult to tell what the exact result of the tariff will be, but I venture to say'that it will raise the cost of living for every man, woman and child in Canada. It will raise the cost of living as a result of the action of the Government which my hon. friend from Brantford supports, and it will raise that cost of living at a time when he has been engaged in trying to persuade the same Government to fix the price of foodstuffs in Canada. And I commend to him the consideration of the monumental nature of his inconsistency in that attitude. It will certainly raise the price of everything that we buy for clothing, everything that we buy for production, and nearly all we buy for food. That is the one certain result of the tariff as it is being imposed by the Government.
The Minister of Finance gets very angry with us on this side of the House if it is even suggested that that is the object of the tariff. Well, I would only say that there are many utterances of hon. gentlemen opposite that would lead us to beli'eve that that would be the effect of the tariff m any case, and that the effect will be produced, not so much by reason of the price of imported goods, as by reason of the price of goods produced in this country. I do not know how many hon. gentlemen noticed the interruption of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) the other evening. I think it was when my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turiff) was speaking. He was talking of the tariff upon axle greese, and my hon. friend from Peel very innocently said: Could not we make all that in Canada? Then, as my hon. friend from Assiniboia pointed out, what becomes of the proposal to get revenue by this means? On the one hand, the Minister of Finance tells us that these new taxes are going to give him $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 for the year- and he calls them war taxes, forsooth, though he has told us already that he is going to borrow all the money for the war- and, on the other hand, the follower of the Minister of Finance tells us that he proposes that as much of these goods as possible should be made in Canada. It is impossible that the tariff should at once raise revenue and promote the industry of the country. It never did so. Wherever the protective tariff is introduced it fails as a revenue producer, as the minister told us this afternoon it must do. The real objection to the tariff legislation of this Government is in
this, that by raising prices to the consumer of . almost everything used in this country, it builds up the fortunes of a limited class of our people at a time when everybody else in this country is learning how to suffer patiently. I pictured in my opening remark the
11	p.m. farmer who has sent 'his son to the front and is left on the iarm to make his living there. To complete the picture I need to introduce between the farmer and his son the gaunt and greedy figure of the tariff beneficiary who is prepared to line his own pockets by the financial suffering of those left at home while the son who has gone into the trenches is shedding his blood for his country. The real iniquity of these proposals at this time is in this, that while every man, woman and child outside of the beneficiaries of the tariff is learning to spell letter by letter, and to write in tears and blood, the word " Sacrifice!" the tariff beneficiary is there with his hands out for his subsidy. I am glad that I stand with those who are prepared to sacrifice and not with those who are seeking subsidies. Then my hon. friend from Victoria, and other hon. gentlemen on that side of the House, with unctuous patriotism on behalf of others say that they are quite sure the farmers of the West will be quite prepared to make their share of sacrifice.
They will.

Yes, their share. They make their sacrifices in sending their sons to the trenches; but they do not propose- the workmen of our towns do not propose -to make a further sacrifice in the case of unjust taxation to the Moloch god of protection. That is the issue between us in regard to this question of tariff taxation and of " sacrifice " which falls so lightly from the lips of hon. members opposite, and I am glad to say falls so thoughtlessly also. The policy of the Government is shortsighted. What is the good of sending lecturers on production all over Canada, and at the same time putting these obstacles in the way of production. Production depends on power to exchange. You erect barriers against international exchange and then go to the farmer and say: Produce more but do not seek markets in which to sell your produce. It would be as rational to say to a man: Breathe freely, it is good for your health; and at the same time to put a string around his windpipe. You

prevent yonr foreign trade by tariffs, and then you say to the farmers: For goodness sake, in these serious times, produce more. Short-sighted '
Now I come to the British preference. The short-sightedness, I think, comes out especially in connection with the British preference. The Minister of Finance put some question to me in regard to the British preference, and indulged in that flippant sophistry which usually finds its expression in the columns of the Toronto News, about the preference not having been lowered. The amendment of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition does not say anything about the preference. It says there are additional obstacles being placed against British trade. That is what the amendment says, and that is what the tariff is doing-putting additional obstacles against British trade. No denial is possible to that simple statement.
Of course, my hon. friend comes along with his arithmetical and proportional calculation and says: but we are not doing so badly to Britain as we are to the other countries of the world. But what consolation is that to Britain? Suppose my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works-which God forbid-had fallen into the hands of the Germans, and his family had fallen into the hands of the Germans with him. Suppose they had said that he was so wicked a character that they would cut off both his hands and gouge out both his eyes; would it have been very much consolation to any remaining member of my hon. friend's family if they had taken from my hon. friend only one hand or only one eye? That is all there is to this childish argument. What is the good of talking about Britain still having a preference in the market if you are making the tariff so high that she cannot compete with our own producers? That is my answer to my hon. friend's economic refinements which he makes with such abundance and such a profuse use of the first personal pronoun.
What was the other question my hon. friend put to me? He said: "Were the duties against British goods raised by my right hon. friend for the purposes of protection?" I am enough of a Scotchman to answer my hon. friend's question by asking him another, and the other question I want to put is' this: if my right hon. friend raised the duty on some specific British import to the point that it became a protective duty, how is my hon. friend going to get a revenue by raising it still higher? I trust that some

of my hon. friend's colleagues will draw his attention to my answer to his question. War taxes? How can these be war taxes? If my right hon. friend made the tax protective and barred the goods from the country, or largely so, are they going to be admitted when my hon. friend raises the tax still higher? They know that there is only one answer to that question; it is a protective tax; it is a tax to protect the home producer. Do not let us hear any more about sacrifice just at this point in the argument.
My hon. friend's policy is short-sighted because, inevitably, we are handing over business to the United States. The United States, we are told, have imposed war taxes, but they have been sensible enough to do so not by way of raising the tariff, but by imposing a very large number of direct taxes. They have found out the fallacy of tariffs over there. It is a piece of absolute folly, hurtful to Canada, to put a tax, for example, on wool, at the very time when the United States are admitting wool free into their country, thus freeing the hands of their manufacturers. If you go to almost any manufacturer in Britain to-day and ask Ixim why he prefers free trade to protection, he will say that it is because as a manufacturer he has done better under free trade. If you ask him why, he will say because of the cheap rate at which he can get his raw material. But in the terrible times through which we are passing and which are still in front of us, the highest wisdom of this Government in restoring the manufacturing industries and the prosperity of the commerce of this country is to be found in their following a road diametrically opposed to the road which has led Britain to the commercial and manufacturing supremacy that she has in the world to-day.
My hon. friend's policy is short-sighted, because after this war every one of us knows that we shall need British capital again. My hon. friend says that the present depression of trade exists because we cannot get capital. I want to call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that he has in his Budget taken the best way to debar British capital from this country. Just as when the British preference was first introduced, goods came and our goods went in payment, which is the basic principle of all international trade, so the people came, capital came and prosperity came. My hon. friend has reversed all this, with the zeal of a pervert.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Don't you believe it.
Don't believe what? Is my hon. friend not putting on these taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not believe the theory that you are putting forward.

I am not dealing in
theories. My hon. friend is the theorist for this Government, and the theory he puts forward to-night in this very connection was the most extraordinary that I ever heard come from a man who professes to be an economist. I hope he will not include me in his class any more; he is in a class absolutely by himself. My hon. friend puts forth the theory to-night that these tariffs of his will not bar out trade. Then what becomes of the " Made in Canada " propa-gandism? I said it was stupid, but it is worse than that if the tariff will not bar out trade. I will have to correct myself and call it wicked as well. Trade, as a rule, is not founded on sentiment. When the Investors' Review and the Economist, both journals of very high standing, animadverted to the disadvantage of the increased obstacles which my hon. friend has put on against British trade, they did not do so on the ground of the effect on Britain. They know something about trade and finance over there, and both these trade journals lamented the increased obstacles against British trade on the very grounds which I have now been bringing before the House; because of their hurtfulness to Canada and the Canadian people. They both support the fiscal policy which has made Britain what she is to-day in the hands of Mr. Lloyd George and his colleagues, who were in Parliament and preaching sound economics at the time when my hon. friend had scarcely escaped from the schoolmaster's rod. These papers lament the fiscal legislation that my hon. friend is introducing because of its hurtfulness to Canada. But I will say that if ever sentiment entered into relations of trade I would have thought it would do so at the present moment in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. This is a view that is being held by large numbers of British people in this country. I have a couple of sentences that were written to me by an Englishman in Winnipeg the other day; the writer will be recognized as an Englishman by the straightforwardness, honesty, sincerity and strength of his speech. He says:
Every one I hear talking thinks it is nothing less than a stab in the back, a real piece of treachery, helping the enemy. To borrow the
whole cost of the war from England and then turn round and tax her goods extra, ostensibly to find the money to repay her, but really to give the tariff hogs a little more swill, is rotten.
That is how Britishers in the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Rogers) are talking about this tariff.
Hon. ROBT., ROGERS:	That gentlemen
is not acquainted with many people out there.	/

My hon. friend' may be
mistaken on that point. In the last election Winnipeg gave a popular majority against the Government of which my hon. friend was once an ornament of about 8,000. My hon. friend should not be too sure about what he knows of the people of Winnipeg. My friend, Mr. Dixon, who was elected en that occasion by the biggest majority ever given, I think, a provincial candidate in Manitoba, is a free-trader and single-taxer, who came originally from the city of Nottingham. There are more people there who have fiscal light than my hon. friend dreams of. The last trial of strength was not very strong in support of the view which has just been expressed by the hon. gentleman, for whom I have a very great regard, so great a regard that I would not like him to live- in a fool's paradise in this matter. Instead of spending his time studying electioneering politics I would recommend that he study economics, and then when he runs up against a propaganda like Dixon's he will be able to deal with it with arguments of a different kind to what are used in practical politics.
I wish the Government even now would repent on this matter of the British preference. I say it sincerely, I would not put a tax on British goods just now; and a man is always sincere when he commends others to take the course he would have taken himself. I would not put an additional obstacle against British goods at this time. I would have been too fearful of linking up myself, even in thought, with what has been done by the enemies of my country. If I may repeat what has been said by my right hon. leader this afternoon: "I would not fight British trade with tariffs at the time that the Germans are fighting it with submarines." It would be most impolitic to do so when British trade is doing so much for the world as it is doing. My hon. friends will tell me it is not Britain's trade, it is the Navy. Of course, it is the Navy. But what built the Navy? Protectionists will never build a navy. The last thing protectionists want is ships. If you

go in for the home market and interprovincial trade, which have failed you so lamentably sCt the present moment, and for the made-in-Canada propaganda you will never build many ships. The Navy is the direct result of trade. It is the final outcome of the commercial and the colonizing and civilizing qualities which are the glory of the British race. British trade is to-day the chief support of the Allies, Mr. Speaker, it is more than that. It is itself the chief ally. It is British trade which is bringing succour to the poor and needy Belgian refugees. It is British trade which is enabling Britain to finance her own outlying dominions and the smaller belligerents states. It is British trade which is keeping open the ports of the North American continent and of all neutral states. It is British trade which is saving to-day the civilized world. Hon. gentlemen opposite think the time fitting to obstruct that trade, and at the same time propose to throw extra burdens on our own people. We on this side of the House most confidently believe that in this most serious crisis it is not wise either to obstruct your commerce or to burden year people.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer a few remarks with regard to the motion now before the House. After listening to the addresses on the Budget that have been delivered here this afternoon and tonight, I can imagine that at this late hour hon. gentlemen are pretty well loaded up with the subject, and that nothing new or interesting can now be said with regard to it. It is just about a month ago that the Budget was delivered in this House. For nearly two weeks we were living in expectation of the Opposition's taking up the discussion of the Budget; hut adjournment after adjournment took place, until finally the financial critic of the Opposition replied. To-day we have listened to an address from the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who has moved an amendment dealing with one phase of the Budget. I believe that at this particular time in our history we should consider the questions that come before Parliament in a sober, serious manner, that matters should not be considered lightly or with levity. I regret to have come to the conclusion that that has not characterized all the addresses that have 'been delivered in this House.
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Michael Clark), after rMr. M. Clark.]
addressing the House for an hour and a half. I have heard him on previous occasions dealing with public questions in this House, and I must say that I have often listened to him with a good deal of interest. But the very fact that to-night he lias not been up to his usual standard is an indication that he found the subject a very difficult one. We all recognize in the hon. member for Red Deer a keen debater, a man with a logical mind who is quick to detect and reach the weak joints in the armour of his opponent; but to-night, if we are to judge by the vehemence and lung power which he displayed, I think he was sadly lacking in the arguments he is usually able to find. I shall attempt to deal with just a few of those he has advanced. We have listened with interest and sometimes with amusement to the arguments he has advanced in favour of that old hobby of his, free trade. We have heard him denounce protection to-night in a manner that would indicate that he was thoroughly sincere in that respect. But the hon. member for Red Deer is somewhat like the parrot that once found himself in difficulties, and who, after coming to a sober realization of the plight he was in, came to the conclusion that he had talked too much. I have heard the hon. member for Red Deer deal with protection from a different standpoint to that which he assumed to-night. I remember that he had made a speech on protection two years ago, and I took the trouble to find out whether he was always the ardent free trader that he is to-day. When I heard him denounce this made-in-Canada propaganda I could not help thinking that I had heard him on a similar subject in the past, and on looking over the records-and you can find his name displayed on almost every page of the records of that year-I found that the hon. gentleman did not always denounce the made-in-Canada movement that we heair so much about to-day. In fact, he championed it, and a very able and eloquent champion he was. I wish to quote a few remarks that he made in this House in March, 1913, which will be found in the Unrevised Hansard, page 4648. He said:
The simple fact is that Canada cannot afford these dreadnoughts, sending money out of the country without recompense in the shape of developing industries within the country.
That was the attitude of the hon. gentleman at that time. Is that the song he sings to-day? No, he preaches an entirely

different doctirine. He was a made-in-Camada man at thalt time.
Is there anything inconsistent between defending my own house against a burglar and buying something from a neighbouring store ?

No, but I am inclined to think that if the people of the British Empire had been of the same opinion as the hon. gentleman on that occasion the burglar would be in possession to-day and we would be paying tribute to our neighbours. We would not be sending our men over to help Britain in the fight that is now engaging the attention of the civilized world. He goes further; he says that of the $91,000,000 of an increase in our trade of the previous year, only $9,000,000 represents the increase in exports. That means that we increased our borrowings to such an extent that our increase in production will barely suffice to pay the interest on our increased borrowings. To-day he says: Buy in the cheapest market and sell wherever you can. He denounced protection and he cited figures down to the year 1895. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that down to the year 1896 when the Liberal Government came into power, they had denounced protection and they had proclaimed what they would do with it if returned to power. Was it any wonder that the manufacturers of the country, that the people who desired to invest money in industrial development, were nervous at the possibility of those gentlemen being connected with the Government of this country? We know as a matter of fact notwithstanding the professions that were made at the time, the manufacturers were privately assured that if hon. gentlemen opposite came into power they would not repeal the protective tariff. Is it to be wondered at that capital obtained confidence after the late Government had been in power a few years? People realized that the protective tariff had come to stay, and that hon. gentlemen opposite were not sincere in their professions when they said they were going to repeal the protective tariff. Confidence having been established in the minds of people interested in manufacturing industries that protection was the policy of both parties, a great development took place between the period to which I refer and the present time. Year after year we have seen industries springing up, and we haye secured the investment of hundreds of millions of dollars in different lines of manufacture. I know that the hon. gentleman from Red Deer does not like to
hear this and in order to get away from a conscience that is troubling him he has, I believe, walked out of the House. I do not intend to devote further time to that subject.
The protective tariff that he has attacked to-night has been attacked also by hon. gentlemen opposite. They still sing that old song that we heard so much of in 1911-[DOT] unrestricted reciprocity. The hon. leader of the Opposition said to-day: In 1911 you debarred us from selling to the United States and now you are going to prevent us from buying from Great Britain. Does he not realize that the markets of the United States are freer to us to-day than they were when reciprocity was an issue? Is it not a fact that we can sell more freely to the United States under the conditions that exist to-day than we could have done had reciprocity come into effect? I have the best of authority for making that statement and I am going to quote my authority. After the Wilson tariff had come into effect, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) was in the United States, and he was calling upon the President. The Globe of November 27, 1913, contains the folowing allusion to this subject:
Representative James R. Mann, the Republican floor leader of the House who has followed Canadian tariff matters closely, was asked what trade relations might be discussed between the Canadian Premier and President Wilton, Mr. Mann said : "I do not see what object Premier Borden could have in discussing trade questions with the President or the present Administration. I cannot understand what more could be obtained by Canada by way of trade benefits than the Dominion can now have under the Underwood tariff law. The United States gave Canada much more in the Underwood tariff reductions than the Canadian reciprocity proposed to give. While the latter Act was intended to be reciprocal, the Underwood Act is not, and Canada does not have to give .anything in return.
That is pretty good authority. Yet in face of that we find that on March 7 of last year the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Le-mieux) who, I am sorry to find, has not been able to attend during the last few days on account of illness, made this statement in a public address delivered at Buffalo:
" If an appeal were made now to the Canadian people," said Mr. Lemieux, " there would be an overwhelming majority in favour of the reciprocity pact.*'
That is also taken from the Globe of March 7, 1914. We had a similar statement from the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon), who is an ardent advocate of reciprocity. I can imagine what the condition of affairs would have been if at the

present time reciprocity had been in existence. With a war in progress in the old land and tariff entanglements that woul(J be bound to create differences between us and the United States, the situation would have been one full of embarrassment. I have not admired the course of the United States during the whole progress of this war, and I am pleased that we have no entanglements, no alliances of any kind, but that we are able to assist the Empire in whatever manner we choose.
I want to call the attention of the House to a remark made by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition in his address this afternoon. He was referring to the truce which he claimed had not been observed on this side of the House. I have heard this question during the past few days discussed in the House. I have been quite of the opinion that there was no truce for some time past, if ever. I heard my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) make a statement that he and the leader of the Opposition had cancelled some meetings which they had intended to hold and that they had observed the truce. I can quite understand why they would cancel meetings at the time the war broke out. I can imagine what sort of a reception the leader of the Opposition would have had if he had gone out through this country holding political meetings at that time in view of the record which he established for himself in preventing Canada from doing her part to assist Britain in strengthening the naval forces of the Empire. He well might withdraw, but the Liberal press in this country, day in and day out, have continued to discuss political questions not at all as if a truce existed but as if they were going to avail themselves of every opportunity of gaining a political advantage. 1 want again to quote from the Toronto Globe which, as the House well knows, is the organ of the Liberal party in the province from which I come. In its editorial column it says:
" Our policy," said Sir Wilfrid, speaking of the attitude of himself and his supporters during the long session, " was that we should have two fleet units, one on the Atlantic and one on the Pacific, to take the places of the British squadrons which had been removed from these waters. . . . We on this side of the House are as ready to bear our burden, to discharge the duty we owe to the Motherland as British subjects, as any others can be; but we want to do it in the manner which was adopted by all parties at one time, when this question was approached free from party bias, by the organization of a Canadian navy on lines compatible with the autonomy of Canada." The

reference here is to the naval debate that grew out of the resolution of Mr. Foster in 1909.
Sir Wilfrid pointed out at some length, and with great clearness and emphasis, the effect of the removal of the North American squadron from the North Atlantic Ocean: all Canadian exports would, in the event of a foreign war, have to pass into and through the United States, to be carried to their destination under the flag of that country. The present war has made plain the prophetic character of this presage. The presence of a few German cruisers meant for a time serious derangement of British commerce, not merely on the Atlantic, but also on the Pacific and Indian Oceans. If Canada had, under the Borden Administration, carried out the Canadian naval policy, in co-operation with Australia and in accordance with the terms of their agreement of 1909, these German cruisers would never have produced a tithe of the alarm and destruction they caused.
This is the Liberal policy as outlined by the Liberal leader in Parliament. It purports to provide for the defence of Canada on both oceans, and also of Australia and New Zealand.
That editorial was contained in the Toronto Globe of November 25, 1914, and other editorials of a similar nature have appeared in that and other papers, all of which goes to show that the Liberals have not been keeping the truce. The Winnipeg Free Press also contained similar statements, one of which I shall read:
Among the nations of the Empire, Australia stands higher now in the sight of all the world by reason of the achievement of the cruiser Sydney of the Australian navy. Canada in 1909 adopted the Canadian navy policy by unanimous vote of the Dominion Parliament, on a resolution moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and seconded by Mr. Borden. This Dominion entered into an agreement with the Commonwealth of Australia to co-operate on the Pacific with Dominion navies. That agreement was abandoned by the present Government of this country. Would it not have been a fine thing if a cruiser of the Canadian navy, say the Winnipeg, had chased down and destroyed the Emden?
I would point out to hon. gentlemen opposite that they have not observed the truce, when their press contains such articles as these by which they are deliberately attempting to mislead and influence the people of this country. In 1909 the three Dominions, Australia, New Zealand and Canada, decided to share the burdens of naval defence. All three Dominions started even and Australia built a whole fleet unit and New Zealand built a battle cruiser in 1909, but down to nearly the end of 1911, when the late Government went out of power, we find that Australia and New Zealand had completed their part of the contract and Canada had not done anything. The Liberal Government did not attempt to do anything with regard to naval defence; it was a matter of procrastination with them. Not a ship was

built, not a keel was laid, not a contract was given by the Liberal Canadian Government during till the time they were in power. To-day they say : why we were just on the verge of doing something when the change of Government took place. I say, Sir, that tenders called for by the late Government were received on the 1st of May, 1911, and shortly after that, on the 12th day of May, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and two of his ministers, went to England to attend the Imperial conference, there to throw cold water on Imperial matters. They arrived back in Ottawa on the 12th of July, the dissolution of Parliament took place on July 29th, and the election was held on the 21st of September. During all these summer months the tenders were lying in the office pigeon-holed, and the Government never made any attempt to let a contract. This showed that they were not sincere in what they were professing to the people of this country; it proved that they had no intention whatever of carrying out the policy they were preaching with regard to naval defence: I believe that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) gave us an insight into what was the custom and habit of the Liberal party, not only when in power, but when in opposition, when the other day he stated in this , House: that he had come to the conclusion that political parties are justified in certain instances in not keeping promises which they never should have made. Is not that a nice doctrine to preach? That political parties should not keep promises which they should never have made. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt) did not go so far as to say that if it was going to have any political effect it might be a good thing to make these promises and to not observe them afterwards. Later on, in his speech, the contention of the hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) was that the present Government should not only ignore what the late Government had done with respect to the building of the Hudson Bay railway, but be done with the whole thing. He indicated that the late Government, although they had made extensive and expensive surveys, and had made a careful estimate as to the resources of the country through which the railway passed, were not absolutely convinced they were justified in building that road. The impression he would leave on the minds of the people is, that this was one of the promises that the late Government would be justified in breaking. In contrast to that, let me point out that at a political meeting at which I was present not very long ago, during the South Huron by-56
election, the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), late Minister of Railways, were present, and if I remember corectly, and l think I do, the hon. member for South Renfrew said:	the
Tory Government we now have in power in this country have done nothing; they have not put any practical legislation on the statute books; it was not they who initiated the Hudson Bay railway, I signed the contract for the building of that road, and all the credit should go to the Liberal Government and not to the present Government. What are we to think when we find a member of the Opposition getting up in this House and asking us to denounce the building of the Hudson Bay railway now, and to disregard the contract that had been entered into by our predecessors? Is that the kind of honour we want to see on the part of governments and political parties in this country? I say no, and I hope that such a damnable doctrine as that will receive the treatment it ought to receive from the people of Canada. That is not the kind of honour we want to see inculcated into the youth of this country? 1 may say that a more pernicious doctrine was never preached by any political man in this country than that which fell from the lips of the hon. member for North Oxford on that occasion.
I want to make a few further references to this truce, which has been violated by the Toronto Globe, by the Winnipeg Free Press, and by almost every Liberal candidate who has been nominated during tho past few months. The most offensive partisanship has been displayed by these gentlemen at these conventions, and it has been published broadcast in the Liberal press throughout Canada. I want to say, Sir, that the record of the Opposition with regard to the construction of the navy is just exactly in keeping with the doctrine that was preached by the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). I want to say, further, that only on January 19 of last year we had a statement from the leader of the Opposition in this House, which gives a pretty fair index of what was in his mind, and, indeed, the same idea was expressed by many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. The right hon. gentleman said:
Emergency? Who speaks to-day of emergency? Twelve months have passed since my right hon. friend the Prime Minister introduced his measure. Twelve months and more have passed since that time when he saw the German peril. He saw Germany almost ready to jump at the throat of Great Britain. He saw clouds



on the horizon; he saw these clouds rent by lightning; he heard the murmurs and rumbling oi distant thunder. But my right hon. friend to-day lives in peace. The atmosphere is pure, the sky is clear.
Those were the predictions of the right hon. gentleman just one year ago. Two years ago he succeeded in defeating the proposition introduced by the Prime Minister of Canada to render some assistance to the British Empire, and to remove the stigma and reproach standing against us to-day that we have never done anything for the Empire; that we have been receiving favours at the hands of Great Britain, and that we have never displayed the manliness to assume a share of the burdens of Empire. When the Prime Minister brought down that measure it was defeated by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and those who sat behind him in this House and by his followers in the Senate. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), who was heartily in accord with the policy of his leader, on the same day, January 19, 1914, made the following statement:
The whole case of contribution was a case of emergency, and the emergency disappeared when the fleet went to Gibraltar. And if it disappeared at that time, where is the emergency to-day? My right hon. friend knows, and every one of his supporters knows, that the fleet has been dispersed to the seven seas and the German fleet with it-and every lover of civilization is very glad to see that come about. And that dispersal of the fleet is the second absolute ' justification of all that the Opposition did last winter, whether it was in the House of Commons or in the Senate.
That shows where the influence exerted in the Senate came from.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition says:	" In Great Britain the Government
have called the Opposition in ' and have consulted with them as to conditions in regard to the war; they have taken them into their councils. He complains: We have not been taken into the councils of this Government; consequently, you need not complain if we criticise you to-day. Let me tell the right hon. gentleman that the attitude of the Opposition in the old country was not the same as the attitude of the Opposition in Canada. They have not displayed the same disposition that has been displayed here year in and year out by hon. gentlemen opposite. During all the years that my hon. friends were in power and during the few years that the present Government has been in power, my hon. friends opposite day in and day out have exerted themselves to prevent Canada from assuming her part

of the burden of the Empire. Is it any wonder, with a record such as that, that the hon. leader of the Opposition was not called into the councils of the Government. He says: Do not complain if to-day we are criticising the course of the present Government. Is it pique that influences the right hon. gentleman? Is he so sensitive because he has been left out that he finds it necessary to criticise the Government on a question of this kind with the Empire engaged in the most serious war that has ever taken place in the history of the world, with millions of men armed to the teeth, with the contesting parties locked together to-day in a death struggle, each realizing full well what defeat or victory will mean to them? Is this a time for a political leader to\ exhibit a disposition of that kind and to complain that because he has not been consulted by the Government, he will criticise it?
The right hon. gentleman occupied most of his time in picturing the grave injustice which would be done to the poor man, and how the wealthy man was going to escape practically scott free. He referred to the tax on railway tickets. He did not tell hon. members that the wealthy man was taxed twice to the poor man's once. The wealthy man is taxed when he purchases his ticket and also when he takes a seat in tile Pullman car. I could not see any force in my right hon. friend's argument. I have taken the trouble to look the matter up, and I am still of the same opinion.
Would my hon. friend not consider it a reasonable proposal that a second-class ticket should bear a smaller rate of taxation than a first-class ticket bears?
I do not see that there is very much difference. As a matter of fact, I think most people travel first-class in this country.
You would get all the more revenue, then.

The principal cause of the trouble with the minister-
That is, the Minister of Militia.
-and his top-heavy militia is the report of a general by the name of French, who came to this country some years ago, and in my judgment his visit was one of the greatest misfortunes that has befallen Canada.
I told the late Minister of Militia publicly and privately that in adopting the ridiculous and unreasonable report made by this gentleman, he had committed a great mistake. It might be all right if General French was reporting on the conditions in Bulgaria, or Russia, or Germany, or even Italy, but when it comes to a country like Canada where there is not a possibility of trouble, his ideas are ridiculous.
