The department brought over a man like General French and he lays out the country in divisional areas. That was not enough and they had to increase the divisional areas and get more officers. He heard a hiss pass through the House at that, and so he said:
-I will take that word back. This English General Inspecting Officer, or whatever you call him. When I was in Germany, I admit that I could see the result of the military training there: you could see it as the men walked alcng the street. In Canada you do not get enough military training for it to be of any benefit physically. All you get in the militia of Canada is that you teach about 25 per cent of the men in Canada how to get drunk.
This was the hon. member for Carleton's estimate of the men who belong to the militia of this country. I say that a more contemptible insult was never hurled at the men wearing the King's uniform. These words are on Hansard, and they will remain a reproach against the hon. member for Carleton as long as he lives and does not volunteer for service in order to remove the reproach that stands against him. And what did we hear from another hon. gentleman, also very close to the late Government, and now one of the chief whips of the party of hon. gentlemen opposite?
The Minister of Militia has not been hoping to bu'ld up a militia which may be and which ought

to be useful; he has been simply building up a militia which may be called out ait any minute. His idea is absolutely wrong, and it is not a good idea for the young people of Canada to grow up with. I am in favour of the militia, but a minister who is in charge of the Militia Department of the Dominion of Canada and who is building up a militia day in and day out along the lines that to-morrow we may be at war with somebody, has not got the right idea in mind and is imbuing the spirit of war into the souls of the people of this Dominion. There Is no question about the necessity of a militia, but why should we spend in militia the enormous sum we are spending to-day is more than I can understand.
Numerous criticisms of this kind were hurled against the militia expenditures and the Minister of Militia. Hon. gentlemen opposite to-day contend that we should reduce the expenditure of this country. Is this one of the items that they want reduced? Have they the hardihood to say: We do not approve the enormous war expenditure you are making? No; they say: We are heartily in sympathy with the voting of $100,000,000 or whatever sum may be required. I ask the hon. member for Bed Deer: Is it not well that the Government should be prepared for the situation which has arisen? If hon. gentlemen opposite were sincere in the professions which they have made during the course of this debate; if they were anxious to unite with the Government of the day in rendering whatever aid they could to the Empire, they would not have made the flimsy criticisms which they have made in connection with the proposals of the Government.
On June 1 last, just two months before the outbreak of war, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) made the following remarks:
I agree that according to his own judgment he has been doing his best.
That is, the Minister of Militia.
But he is far too enthusiastic in the course he is pursuing. He is far ahead of his time; in fact, the time will never come in this country when the- expenditure he proposes will be justifiable.
Mr. Sam. Hughes:	Take care; do not be too
sure.
Mr. Guthrie: I do not take much stock in these warnings given by the minister at Victoria and Toronto as reported by the newspapers in those cities. We must realize and I am sure his colleagues do realize-that this is a country of peace and not of war.
These are the sentiments of hon. gentlemen opposite as expressed before war was declared. They criticised with all the vigour which they could command the estimates of the Militia Department. What do they say to-day? The hon. member for South Well-

ington said that he did not take much stock in the statements made by the Minister of Militia at Victoria and Toronto. Have they not turned out to be correct? Is there a man in this House or in this country who will say that the Minister of Militia from the outset has not displayed wonderful foresight and organizing ability in connection with the mobilizing of the troops at Valcar-tier a few weeks after war was declared? After the troops had been drilling, shooting and undergoing strict discipline for a few weeks, a murmur of impatience arose from many hon. gentlemen opposite because the troops were not being hurried to the front. I believe it would have been better if the men had remained at Valcartier longer than they did; the training that they were undergoing there was hardening them for the work which they will have to do. The unfortunate weather conditions which they encountered when they crossed the water were such as even the authorities in Great Britain could not be expected to foresee, and I believe that the men were not physically as fit when they went to the front as when they left the Canadian shores. But it is to-day a standing compliment to this Government and to the Minister of Militia that these troops were mobilized and sent to the front in such a satisfactory manner. I want to say that if there is a man in the country who objects to the war tax, the best thing he can do is volunteer for service at the front. The men who are prepared to pay the taxes realize that they are not making much of a sacrifice compared with that which is being made by the men who have gone to the front.

The hon. gentleman says that gentlemen on this side of the House or anywhere in the country who oppose this Budget ought to volunteer for active service. May I ask the hon. gentleman why he does not volunteer himself?

I am not objecting to the sacrifice that hon. gentlemen opposite are objecting to; that is just the point I want to emphasize. The man who objects to contributing by way of taxation to the defence of the Empire ought to volunteer for active service and thus show that he is prepared to make some real, actual sacrifice.
No one is objecting to the war tax, so far as I know. I never heard of any objection.
It is the so-called war tax to which we object.

That brings me
back to the matter that I thought had been effectively cleared up by the Minister of Finance this afternoon.
There are two resolutions on the Order Paper, one relating to a war loan, and the other to domestic affairs. I should like to hear my hon. friend's opinion of the one relating to domestic affairs.

During the course of his remarks the junior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) said:
I understand hon. gentlemen opposite to contend that the falling revenue and the fresh taxation imposed is due to the war. If I am not correct in this, let the correction come now. At any rate, this point is worthy of investigation. I personally do not believe that our loss in revenue is in any substantial degree attributable to the war.
The hon. gentleman does not believe that the falling revenues are in any degree attributable to the war. Yet the revenues of the United States, a country which is in a position to reap enormous benefits from the war; a nation which has shown no inability to take advantage of opportunities to make financial gain, have been galling to such an extent that they have been obliged to resort to war taxes. Some months previous to the war large financial concerns in this country suddenly began to experience a condition that was somewhat unusual.
Several months before war was declared one of the largest transportation companies in the world, with most of its assests in Canada, experienced a condition of affairs that to many seemed unfathomable. How was that? It was owing to the fact that for months previous to the declaration of war, early in August last, it was decided by those responsible for the war that the war should take place in the near future, if the date had not actually been fixed. We find that the stock of the Canadian Pacific railway, one of the greatest corporations in the world, had fallen from $280 per share to as low, recently, as $155 per share. What was the effect upon the other large transcontinental lines in this country which had not developed traffic to the same extent as the Canadian Pacific railway, and which did not possess the wealth of that company? The condition of these other lines was such that they had to come to the Government for assistance; and in order to prevent these roads from going into the hands of a receiver the Government found it necessary to do something in order to carry them over for the time. Hon. gentlemen opposite are well aware of that. They know perfectly

portation. I said that there were three transcontinental railways nearing completion, with the Hudson Bay railway also under construction, with nothing like sufficient traffic to keep them busy, and that under these circumstances it would also be impossible for us to have low rates. We have pursued a most reckless iand extravagant policy in regard to our railway construction, and the question is one that [DOT]requires to be most carefully considered by Parliament and the people. I do not envy the task which confronts my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) in regard to these matters. We know that as a matter of fact the eastern portion of the transcontinental railway should never have been built, and that if the policy that the present right hon. Prime Minister had at that time in mind of extending the Intercolonial, upon which this country has expended enormous sums of money, westward to the lakes, had been adopted, it would have been more in the interests of Canada. That would not meet with the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite. They did not wish to encourage the Government ownership of railways. No, they would prefer to give some rich corporation advantages in that respect. Previous to the election of 1911, hon. gentlemen opposite who were then in power, guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway for that portion of their line from Montreal west to Port Arthur, to the extent of $35,000,000. Their action on that occasion made it necessary for the present Government to again come to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway, and everything that has since been done in that respect is a sequence of the course of hon. gentlemen opposite previous to the election of 1911.
We have heard considerable criticism of this Budget from hon. gentlemen opposite, who have declared that the proposals contained in it are not in the interest of the people generally and the farmers particularly. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) was very strong on axle grease. He said: They are going actually to increase the British rate on axle grease. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was very strong on squid. He thought it was a terrible thing to increase the duty on squid. It seems that fertilizer was what he had in his mind.

I think it is out of order at half-past twelve o'clock for the 
hon. gentleman to indulge in untruthful remarks.

I made no reference to the duty on squid. What I called attention to was the fact that squid had been made free, and the Government was boasting as to that. They had put a duty on fertilizers and many other things, and they were claiming credit for making squid and one other article free.

It is quite evident, judging from the last remarks of the hon. gentlemen, that he is a little bit hazy yet as to what he did say. I have a distinct recollection that he associated squid with the fertilizers, and I think other hon. gentlemen who heard him will bear out my recollection. I want to say, Sir, that the increase in the duty on raw materials and free imports made it necessary that the tariff should be increased on the finished products. That is quite clear to every one who looks at the matter with an unprejudiced mind. So far I fail to have received a single objection from any one of my constituents against the Budget proposal, and indeed I have failed to see even a serious criticism of the Budget in the press of the country. I think it is a great compliment to the Minister of Finance that his proposals have been received in the manner in which they have by the people of Canada, and I deeply regret that hon. gentlemen opposite have not displayed a different spirit towards the policy of the Government at this particular time in the history of the Empire.
I could understand them if they said: We do not approve of what you are doing, hut in view of the seriousness of the situation, and in view of the fact that it is necessary for us to present a united front to the enemy and to assist the Motherland in every possible way in this crisis, we will defer our criticism for a future occasion. Had they done that, I think their action would have commended itself better to the people of this country. Let me commend to these hon. gentlemen opposite the patriotic words of Kipling:
Oh, East is East and West is West,
And never the two shall meet,
Till earth and sky stand presently At God's great judgment seat.
But there is neither East nor West,
Border, nor breed, nor birth,
Where two strong men stand face to face, Though they come from the ends of the earth.

Had the right hon. leader of the Opposition met the leader of the Government in this spirit, he would, in my opinion, stand much higher in the opinion of all Canadians than he does now.
Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Guysborough): It is a very late hour for me to ask the indulgence of the House for a short time. My great difficulty in answering my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) is not on account of the argument he has put before the House, but on account of the tact that he has been speaking to the wrong resolution. If you will refer, Mr. Speaker, to the order paper you will find there are two resolutions, one which relates to ways and means, and which concerns altogether our domestic affairs, and the other which relates to the borrowing of $100,000,000 to carry on the war. The resolution that is before the House is that relating to our domestic affairs, and the second resolution has not even been moved yet. When that resolution is called, I am quite sure it will pass without a dissenting voice; but it is a curious thing that my hon. friend has made a two hours' speech on a resolution that has not yet been called. Why should we have from him a long speech about dreadnoughts and about war, on a resolution that is not yet before the House? I think I can suggest a reason, and I think that reason is that this domestic resolution which we are discussing involves some explanation from Government supporters which my hon. friend is not prepared to give. For example, there is a deficit of $80,000,000 in connection with our domestic affairs, and it was due to the House that the hon. gentleman should have endeavoured to explain that. He did not do so, but he treated us to a long dissertation about dreadnoughts and matters that have no concern at all with what we are now discussing. My hon. friend must not think that he can answer criticisms of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House by telling us that the British and Allied fleets are pounding their way through the Dardanelles. That is a fact, and we are glad to know it, and we join with my hon. friend in wishing them Godspeed, and I may tell him that we are doing just as much to help them along as he or any other member on that side of the House.
I do not want to say anything at this stage that will open up old sores, but if I did venture to make a remark I might say that if my hon. friend and the Government
that he supports had not made a football of the Canadian navy for party purposes, we would have at least four light cruisers of the style of the Australian light cruiser Sydney which did such splendid work in this war, to keep the trade routes open for British commerce, and to assist the old land in the struggle.

Why did you not
build them?

The dreadnoughts
which my hon. friend is talking about could not be ready for use at the present time. The contest in this House in regard to dreadnoughts took place in 1913. Perhaps it will be news to my hon. friend that the Queen Elizabeth, the newest dreadnought of the British fleet, was launched in 1912 and that it has taken the mechanics of Great Britain from that day until a month or two ago to prepare her for the work she is doing now in the Dardanelles. The dreadnoughts spoken of by my hon. friend would be to-day on the stocks in some shipyard in Great Britain, even if the Government had got their policy approved of, whereas if the Government which he supports had gone on with the Canadian navy proposed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we would have at least four ships to assist the old country in the fight which is now raging.
The question as to the truce between the two parties has been discussed a good deal in this House. My hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) has made the statement at a meeting in his city that there is no truce, and that there never was a truce. I beg to differ from him. No hon. gentleman who listened to the discussion which took place at the special session in August last, could come to the conclusion that there was no truce. My hon. leader on that occasion stated the position that the Opposition took in regard to this matter, and it was accepted very kindly by the leader of the Government and he complimented the leader of the Opposition on the patriotic stand he had taken in declaring that we should show a united front to the world in this awful struggle. They both acted on the truce that was then entered into, the proof of which was seen in the case of the by-elections. No candidates were put up in any of the constituencies in these elections, showing that it was well understood by both the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition that there was a truce between the parties at the time. This side of the House never had any notice from

the loader of the Government that the truce was broken, until we saw the speech of my hon. friend published in the newspapers. The question the people of this country are asking is: Is this Government really desirous to devote their# whole attention to the war, or do they regard it of more importance to score another victory against the Liberal party than they do to defeat the Kaiser.
Is that the position they take? In Great Britain it is well understood and well known that there will be no election until after the war is over. As a result there is no party strife. Mr. Speaker, what would you think of the British Government if you were forced to the conclusion that they thought more of their salaries and of their places than they did of the fate of the Empire at such a time as this? I would like to have the same opinion of the Canadian Government as I have of the British Government, but if there is to be a truce, it ought to be a fair and honourable truce, and it ought to apply to both parties. There were indications in October last that the Government was preparing for an election. Large quantities of Conservative literature were sent out from the Conservative headquarters at Ottawa. A number of Conservative conventions were called in the West at the same time. The word was passed around to the faithful in the country. In the maritime provinces there was straws showing how the wind was blowing. It has been the custom in the maritime provinces for many years that the repairs to the Intercolonial should be done in the summer time, when the days are long and the weather fine; but to the astonishment of every one, the order came in the month of October, as I understand, to start out the working gangs on the Intercolonial.

Mr. SINCLAIR; I should like to know from the hon. gentleman who says " hear, hear," what claim the Tory party has to the title of the Imperialistic party? What did they ever do to entitle them to the name? If anybody knows anything that the Conservative party ever did to entitle them

to that name, I wish he would stand up and tell us about it. There has been one step and only one taken since Confederation that had imperialistic significance, one step that touched the imagination and won the applause of men of British blood the world over. That step, as you will remember, was greeted with enthusiasm by England's great Imperial poet and by Her great Imperial statesman, the late Joseph Chamberlain. You will understand that I refer to the British preference. And this " Imperialistic " party supported by my hon. friend from North Ontario voted against the British preference.
There are two incidents of recent Canadian history that everybody remembers. The Tory party four years ago hitched up with the National party of Quebec. Now, it is a matter of history that the leader of the Natonalist party dictated the names of three members of the first Cabinet of the right hon. leader of this Government. Why did the leaders of the Nationalist party leave the Liberal party? The reason given in the province of Quebec is that the Liberal leader was too British for them; and in searching about for some party that .was less British than my honoured leader, they allied themselves with hon. gentlemen opposite. I hope they feel at home there. We have a saying in our part of the Dominion, and I have no doubt that you have it in Ontario, that birds of a feather flock together. This "Imperialistic" party took to their bosom the gentleman who said it was necessary to shoot holes in the British flag in order to be free. They showered honours upon him, first making him Deputy Speaker, and then taking him into the Cabinet and giving him a seat at the Council board. I suppose that is regarded as an Imperialistic move by my hon. hot-air friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sam. Sharpe). That is incident number one. Number two is this present proposal to add 5 per cent to the tax on all British goods. Is this a time to strike a blow at the trade of Great Britain, when the old country is engaged in a struggle for her very 1 a.m. existence? With the enormous increase in freight rates and war insurance this 5 per cent is a heavy addition to the expense of doing trade at present between Great Britain and Canada. If hon. gentlemen will go to the reading room and turn up the files of the New York Herald, they will see that four or five months ago grain could be carried from New York to Liverpool at 2s. 6d. a quarter, and to-day it takes 7s. 6d. a 
quarter to carry the same grain. Hates of insurance have gone up enormously. So the handicaps against British trade are so great that it is almost impossible to carry on business with Great Britain at all. And on top of all this hon. gentlemen opposite come in with a 5 per cent additional tax on British goods. One can imagine the astonishment with which the news was heard in London, especially when a few months before the British Government had agreed to advance to the Canadian Government the whole war expenditure to be made by this country. I think I can see the blush on the face of the Canadian High Commissioner when he handed in the news to the British Government. One can imagine the feelings of the Kaiser when he heard the news that he had another ally in addition to the Turks, when he learned that he would not need submarines to stop trade between Canada and the old country, but that the Canadian Government would see to it that British trade would be crippled. One does not like to speak of it. Tell it not in Vienna, publish it not in the streets of Berlin, lest the daughters of the enemy rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised Hun triumph. Does my hon. friend from North Ontario regard that as an imperialistic move ? I am glad to say that the Commonwealth of Australia has taken a different course; it has taken the patriotic course and is not interfering with the tariff on British goods. Australia, like Canada, found it necessary to raise money, and in December they made a new tariff. They increased their general tariff from five to ten per cent on a large number of imports, hut almost without exception they have left British imports without an increase. There is no flag-waving party in Australia. Australia is British in the true sense of the word. As has already been remarked in the House to-night, there is more than one way in which Canada can take a lesson from the Commonwealth of Australia.
We all recognize that Canada is passing through a period of hard times. We may differ about the -cause. Statesmen on this side of the House saw the depression coming prior to 1911, and they endeavoured to provide for it by opening new markets for Canadian products. Their efforts were frustrated, and Canada is having a taste of the depression that existed prior to 1896. There is -a disposition on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite to attribute the hard times to the war. Everybody who

has a good memory knows that that is not true. It will not be denied that real estate began to decline early in 1913. The receipts of the great railway corporations fell off long before the war. The Customs revenue began to decline about twelve months before the war broke out. In December, 1913, some of the large industrial concerns in Montreal closed their doors and thousands of men were turned out of employment.
Is it not a fact that the financial conditions prevailing in 19i2 were directly due to the war which was then taking place in Europe?
What war was that?
The Balkan war.

Hon. gentlemen opposite promised a reduction in expenditure. Some hon. gentlemen have had the hardihood to deny this, but we can produce the proof. The leader of the Conservative party on August 15, 1911, published in the Montreal Gazette the manifesto of the party, upon which the election was run. It was headed:	" Conservative Policy; what the Party is Pledged to carry out." I quote the first paragraph:
The Liberal Conservative party gives its pledge to carry out the following policy if returned to power:
1.	A thorough reorganization of the method by which the public expenditure is supervised. The increase in what is known as ordinarily controllable expenditure from $21,500,000 in 1896 to nearly $74,000,000 in 1911 is proof of extravagance beyond all possible defence.
A long list of other pledges and promises follow, and the whole is signed " R. L. Borden." There is the pledge, Mr. Speaker, but where is the fulfilment? Upon what occasions have the Government made any attempt to live up to that promise? Has there been any attempt to effect a thorough reorganization of the method of supervising expenditure? I venture to say that never since the days of McGreevy and Connolly has there been so little supervision of expenditure as there is to-day.
The Auditor General is supposed to look after grafters and persons who are trying to rob the treasury, but he is now busy looking after the ministers. The Auditor General recognized that in times of war, the Government must have a freer hand; accordingly, he arranged with them that Orders in Council would be issued authorizing special expenditures. But the Government did not adhere to that arrangement. For months the Department of Militia spent money right and left without any supervision whatever, and after the illegal expenditure had reached the sum of about $5,000,000 the Auditor General had to step in and refuse credit to the Finance Minister. This is what the Auditor General said:
This is a clear violation of the War Appropriation Act, and also of the understanding on which X consented to the issue of a letter of credit. I have, therefore, to request that you will inform the Department of Militia that their letter of credit is no longer available for payments on account of war appropriation, and to further cheques may be drawn for the purpose

1	regret the necessity for this action, but I have no other course open to me. I know it is a very serious matter to place any obstacle in the way of the Militia Department when the country is at war, and with this in view I consented to an arrangement which could not in any degree hamper the department. In return I had every right to expect that the Minister of Militia and Defence would not only carry out the agreement of his officials, but that he would also respect the direction of Parliament
(Signed) J. Fraser,
Auditor General.
So far as I know, the Finance Minister made no reply to that statement. But there you have the practice of the department; and I submit that that is supervision with a vengeance. I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
